# Understanding what's on a page

Day 2, 11:30 · Gary Illyes, Search Relations · coverage: transcript, slides, video

Speaker from the author's recording label. Opened with Slido quiz questions, then the part on main content, which only a second attendee recording captured.

## Claims

- **[Slide]** A Google slide labelled the parts of an example blog page, marking the header and the navigation as not so important and the main content as very important.
  <br><sub>`D2-C309` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [What is canonicalization](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization) · Repeats [D2-C028](../day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extended by [D2-C861](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's canonicalization guide says that when Google indexes a page it determines the page's primary content, which it also calls the centerpiece, and clusters pages whose primary content is the same or very similar.
  > "When Google indexes a page, it determines the primary content (or centerpiece) of each page."
  <br><sub>`D2-C310` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · is the documentation · [What is canonicalization](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`, the glossary term *Main content (centerpiece)*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes pointed to Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines as the detailed source on how Google thinks about the main content of a page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C311` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content), [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Extended by [D3-C170](../day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** When Google processes a page for indexing, it gives words different weights depending on the part of the page where they appear.
  <br><sub>`D2-C312` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Google Search Essentials](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials) · Used by `DEV-HTM-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Words in the footer of a page get a lower weight, so text placed in the footer is unlikely to contribute much to ranking the page.
  > "if you put something in a footer, it's more likely that it's not going to contribute much to ranking"
  <br><sub>`D2-C313` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-HTM-02`</sub>

- **[Slide]** On Google's example blog page, the post title and opening sentence counted as important because they sit in the main content, in front of the user, while the site tagline, the 'Categories' sidebar and category links such as 'Hugo (7)' counted as less important supplementary text.
  <br><sub>`D2-C314` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf), [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) · Used by `DEV-HTM-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** To make a word count for ranking a page, Gary Illyes said the simplest step is to move it into the main content, because where text sits on a page already contributes quite a bit to ranking.
  > "where you position text on a page will already contribute quite a bit to ranking that page"
  <br><sub>`D2-C315` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Google Search Essentials](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials) · Used by `DEV-HTM-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said not everything on a page can or should be important: if everything were placed in the main content, nothing would stand out as main content, which he called working as intended.
  <br><sub>`D2-C316` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Put the terms a page should rank for in its main content (title, headings, opening paragraphs) rather than only in sidebars, tag lists or footers; footer keyword blocks are unlikely to add ranking value.
  <br><sub>`D2-C317` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · Used by `DEV-HTM-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google does not store the complete sentences or the full HTML of a page in the Search index, because large pieces of text would be unsearchable; it tokenizes the text into the smallest segments that still allow search.
  <br><sub>`D2-C318` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D2-C721](../day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Extended by [D3-C109](../day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) · Used by the glossary term *Tokenization*</sub>

- **[Stage]** For languages written with spaces between words, such as English and German, Search tokenization splits a sentence into its individual words.
  <br><sub>`D2-C319` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Text in languages written without spaces, such as Thai and Chinese, would end up in the index as long strings that might never be searched for, so Google segments it into words with statistical models built from other web content in that language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C320` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C011](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Repeated by [D3-C070](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For languages written without spaces, such as Thai and Chinese, Google uses exactly the same word segmentation when indexing a page as when interpreting the user's query, because otherwise the query could not be matched against the index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C321` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D2-C737](../day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Extended by [D3-C013](../day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said a colleague, John, would cover how Google interprets the words of a query on the morning of Day 3.
  <br><sub>`D2-C322` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes)</sub>

- **[Stage]** When tokenizing for Search, Google attaches metadata to each token for use in ranking, such as whether the word appeared in the header or in the main content (tagged 'centerpiece' on the slide), in bold or in a heading; Gary Illyes said he was not showing all of the metadata.
  <br><sub>`D2-C323` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D2-C720](../day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Used by `DEV-HTM-07`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google also stores spam metadata with the tokens of a page, for example that text was white on a white background, so ranking can use that information.
  <br><sub>`D2-C324` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-HTM-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Tokenization for AI models such as Gemini, in training and in inference, differs from tokenization for Search, although Gary Illyes qualified this with 'or mostly'.
  <br><sub>`D2-C325` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Contradicts [D1-C039](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** In tokenization for AI models, common English words stay whole and each maps to a numeric token ID, so the model works with IDs rather than with the words; on Google's slide the word 'can' had the same ID, 740, both times it appeared.
  <br><sub>`D2-C326` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Understand and count tokens](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens) · Used by the glossary term *Tokenization*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Tokenizers for AI models split long words into sub-word pieces that may make no sense on their own, because a token for every possible word would make the vocabulary too big, and a generative model only cares about closeness in vector space.
  <br><sub>`D2-C327` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Understand and count tokens](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens) · Used by the glossary term *Tokenization*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's two tokenization slides showed the difference on the same sentence: the Search tokenizer kept 'robots.txt' and 'tl;dr' as single tokens, while the AI-model tokenizer split them into pieces such as 'tl' and 'dr' or 'robots' and 'txt', with the punctuation as separate tokens.
  <br><sub>`D2-C328` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Day 1's slide said Gemini shares technologies such as tokenization with Search, while on Day 2 Gary Illyes showed that the two tokenizers split the same text differently ('or mostly'); read this as a shared processing step with different outputs, so Search's word tokens and Gemini's sub-word tokens are not the same units.
  <br><sub>`D2-C329` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said the common SEO advice to chunk content for AI systems is misunderstood: chunking is real, but it matters at the level of an AI model's context window.
  <br><sub>`D2-C330` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) · Extends [D1-C054](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by `M-002`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said Gemini's context window, where chunking actually matters, holds millions of tokens.
  <br><sub>`D2-C331` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Long context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context) · Extended by [D2-C869](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `M-002`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gemini does not need content cut into small chunks of 100 or 200 words, Gary Illyes said, since a smaller book fits in its context window.
  <br><sub>`D2-C332` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide), [Long context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context) · Extends [D1-C054](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extended by [D2-C825](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-03`, `M-002`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes added that, once chunk size is thought of in millions of tokens as Gemini's context window allows, chunking has perhaps lost its meaning anyway.
  <br><sub>`D2-C825` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C332](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-03`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Do not rewrite pages into short, self-contained chunks for AI systems; Google says Gemini reads context windows of millions of tokens, so structure content for readers, with clear headings and complete explanations.
  <br><sub>`D2-C333` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · Used by `DEV-AIF-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A soft 404 is a page that should return an error status code but returns HTTP 200; from a crawling point of view it looks indexable, but because it has no real content Google throws it out of the index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C334` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [Troubleshoot Google Search crawling errors](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/troubleshoot-crawling-errors) · Repeats [D1-C073](../day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Extends [D1-C070](../day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Repeats [D1-C355](../day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Extended by [D2-C903](../day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) · Extended by [D2-C700](../day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) · Used by `DEV-ERR-01`, `DEV-ERR-03`, the glossary term *Soft 404*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Because error pages are worded in endless variations, of which 'page not found' is only the classic one, Google cannot detect soft 404s with simple error, word or keyword matching.
  <br><sub>`D2-C335` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google listed four common causes of soft 404s: pages that look like errors but are not, thin or empty content, server or CMS misconfigurations, and JavaScript-dependent content that fails to load.
  <br><sub>`D2-C336` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [Troubleshoot Google Search crawling errors](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/troubleshoot-crawling-errors) · Extends [D1-C073](../day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Extends [D2-C213](../day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-ERR-03`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Mistakes in Google's own systems are a further cause of soft 404s, and Gary Illyes asked site owners to report such mistakes in Google's forums.
  > "BONUS: Mistakes in Google's systems (that you should notify us about)"
  <br><sub>`D2-C337` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google detects soft 404s with a language model, described as something like BERT, that is trained to understand the structure and layout of a page as well as its language, instead of reading the page as one flat wall of text.
  > "This is basically an LLM thing, something like BERT, that is specifically trained to understand page structure"
  <br><sub>`D2-C338` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C042](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For soft 404 detection, the position of error text decides: an error in a less important part such as the navigation need not make a page a soft 404, but an error message alone in the main content, like 'Error establishing a database connection', does, much as a human would judge it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C339` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C078](../day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Used by `DEV-ERR-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's soft 404 detection tells the page chrome, such as navigation and footer, apart from the main content by analysing the page's visual hierarchy alongside its text.
  <br><sub>`D2-C340` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said soft 404 detection keeps searchers from clicking into dead ends and avoids wasting site owners' resources on visitors sent to error pages.
  <br><sub>`D2-C341` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Troubleshoot Google Search crawling errors](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/troubleshoot-crawling-errors)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.
  <br><sub>`D2-C342` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · Used by `DEV-ERR-03`, `DEV-SRV-03`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Hidden text is recorded at token level: Google stores spam metadata such as white-on-white text with the tokens, so leftover hidden keyword blocks are a liability, not neutral clutter, and should be removed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C343` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · Used by `DEV-HTM-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said that whatever a site puts in its navigation or header tells Google the site does not particularly care about that content: it may help users do something on the side, but it is not what the page wants them to do, read or take away.
  <br><sub>`D2-C861` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Extends [D2-C309](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes defined a page's main content as any part of the page that directly helps the page achieve its purpose, what it was built for.
  > "Main content is any part of the page that directly helps the page achieve its purpose"
  <br><sub>`D2-C862` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`, the glossary term *Main content (centerpiece)*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Main content is not only text: images, videos, a tool or anything else that helps a page achieve its purpose can be main content.
  <br><sub>`D2-C863` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Content created by other users can be main content: on a user-generated content site, the user-generated content can be the page's main content.
  <br><sub>`D2-C864` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A comment section below a blog post can still be part of the page's main content and can contribute to Google's understanding of the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C865` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Content inside tabs, for example separate tabs for a product description and a manufacturer description, might be part of a page's main content.
  <br><sub>`D2-C866` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Extends [D2-C202](../day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A page's main content includes all of its headings and its visible title.
  <br><sub>`D2-C867` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf), [Google Search Essentials](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said the main content is what Google considers when ranking a page.
  > "It's the main content that we consider for ranking."
  <br><sub>`D2-C868` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Google Search Essentials](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials), [What is canonicalization](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization) · Extends [D2-C028](../day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Right after saying Gemini's context window holds millions of tokens, Gary Illyes put its size at perhaps 900,000 or even closer to a million, without a unit that the recordings capture.
  > "the context window is perhaps 900,000 or even closer to a million big"
  <br><sub>`D2-C869` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Long context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context) · Extends [D2-C331](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-03`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines define main content as any part of the page that directly helps it achieve its purpose, including text, images, videos, page features such as calculators and content created by users, and they count the title at the top of the page as part of it.
  > "Main Content is any part of the page that directly helps the page achieve its purpose."
  <br><sub>`D2-C870` · Google Search Quality Rater Guidelines (PDF, 11 September 2025) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · is the documentation · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`, the glossary term *Main content (centerpiece)*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines say navigation links are a common type of supplementary content, and that content behind tabs and user reviews or comments may count as main content on some pages and as supplementary content on others, depending on the page's purpose.
  <br><sub>`D2-C871` · Google Search Quality Rater Guidelines (PDF, 11 September 2025) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · is the documentation · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The talk gave Gemini's context window both as millions of tokens and as roughly 900,000 to a million; Google's long-context docs say Gemini models have context windows of 1 million or more tokens (about eight average novels per million), so plan with about one million tokens as the documented floor rather than several million.
  <br><sub>`D2-C872` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page</sub>
